\chapter{Taking, Thinking, Helping, Loving}
\label{ch:ar-taking-thinking-helping-loving}
\hlchaptermodality{32}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say the Arabic for 'he took', 'he thought', 'he helped' and 'he loved', and tell a plain verb from a rebuilt one — doubled, stretched or prefixed — by what the shape does to the root's meaning.}

Say the chapter's four verbs against the four shapes they wear — ʾakhadha plain, fakkara doubled, sāʿada stretched, ʾaḥabba prefixed — then run the done-to shape across maktūb, maʾkhūdh and maḥbūb and restate the ma- engine dhahaba opened.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ʾakhadha]{\ar{أخذ} (ʾakhadha) — \textquotedblleft{}he took,\textquotedblright{} and the last of the plain verbs}

\label{lesson:AR-C32-akhadha}



\begin{quote}
The last chapter changed the \textbf{vowels} inside a root. This one changes the \textbf{shape} of the verb itself — a doubled letter, a stretched vowel, a prefix. The verb here is the plain one, kept to measure the other three against.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
No new letters, and three worth re-reading:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{أ}} — hamza on its \emph{alif} seat, opening the word as it opens \textbf{\ar{أكل}}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{خ}} (\emph{khāʾ}) — the hook family's \textbf{one dot above}, the \emph{ch} of Scottish \textquotedblleft{}loch.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\ar{ذ}} (\emph{dhāl}) — \emph{dāl} with \textbf{one dot above}, the \emph{th} of \textquotedblleft{}this,\textquotedblright{} the letter that opened \textbf{\ar{ذهب}}.
\end{itemize}

Right to left: \emph{ʾa-kha-dha}. Note what the page does with it. \textbf{\ar{كتب}} ran as one unbroken piece; \textbf{\ar{أخذ}} cannot, because \emph{alif} is a non-joiner. It breaks into \textbf{\ar{أ}} and \textbf{\ar{خذ}} — the two-piece shape of \textbf{\ar{ذهب}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{أَخَذَ}} (\emph{ʾakhadha}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{he took}.\textquotedblright{} Root \textbf{\ar{أ}-\ar{خ}-\ar{ذ}}, the plain \textbf{\ar{فَعَلَ}} shape — the last verb in this book to wear it unaltered.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{أَخْذ}} (\emph{akhdh}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{taking}.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\ar{آخِذ}} (\emph{ākhidh}) — \textquotedblleft{}one \textbf{taking},\textquotedblright{} the \textbf{doer} shape of \emph{kātib}, where the root's own \emph{alif} and the pattern's fuse into long \textbf{\ar{آ}} — the fusion seen in \textbf{\ar{آكِل}} (\emph{ākil}), \textquotedblleft{}an eater.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\ar{مَأْخوذ}} (\emph{maʾkhūdh}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{taken},\textquotedblright{} the \textbf{done-to} shape of \emph{maktūb}.
\end{itemize}

Its Hebrew twin is \textbf{\he{אָחַז}} (\emph{ʾaḥaz}), \textquotedblleft{}he seized.\textquotedblright{} Two regular swaps carry you across: Arabic \textbf{\ar{خ}} answers Hebrew \textbf{\he{ח}}, and Arabic \textbf{\ar{ذ}} answers Hebrew \textbf{\he{ז}}. Those are standing correspondences between the languages, not guesses about this pair. English took nothing from either.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the letters — hamza on alif, khāʾ, dhāl — \textquotedblleft{}ʾakhadha,\textquotedblright{} he took
  \item the same opening — \ar{أكل}, then \ar{أخذ}, hamza on its alif seat
  \item which words break — kataba into one piece, ʾakhadha and dhahaba into two
  \item the dot that makes dhāl — dāl, then dhāl, the th of \textquotedblleft{}this\textquotedblright{}
  \item the fused alif — ākil, an eater; ākhidh, one taking
  \item the done-to pair — maktūb, written; maʾkhūdh, taken
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter keeps \textbf{\ar{أخذ}} from running as one piece, and which Chapter 31 verb did run as one? (\textbf{The \emph{alif}}, a non-joiner — against \textbf{\ar{كتب}}.) What turns \textbf{\ar{د}} into \textbf{\ar{ذ}}? (\textbf{One dot above} — \emph{d} becomes the \emph{th} of \textquotedblleft{}this.\textquotedblright{}) Which two words fuse their alifs into \textbf{\ar{آ}}? (\emph{\textbf{Ākil}} and \emph{\textbf{ākhidh}}.) Which Hebrew consonants answer Arabic \textbf{\ar{خ}} and \textbf{\ar{ذ}}? (\textbf{\he{ח}} and \textbf{\he{ז}} — in \textbf{\he{אָחַז}}, \emph{ʾaḥaz}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[fakkara]{\ar{فكّر} (fakkara) — \textquotedblleft{}he thought,\textquotedblright{} and a root rebuilt by doubling}

\label{lesson:AR-C32-fakkara}



\begin{quote}
Every verb so far has been a bare root with vowels poured between its letters. Arabic can also \textbf{rebuild} a root, and the first way it does so is by doubling one letter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ar{ف}}, \textbf{\ar{ك}} and \textbf{\ar{ر}} are all yours, and all three join, so \textbf{\ar{فكّر}} runs as one piece.

The new thing is not a letter but a mark: \textbf{\ar{ّ}} (\emph{shadda}), the little \emph{w} riding the \textbf{\ar{ك}} of \textbf{\ar{فَكَّرَ}}. It says \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{sound this consonant twice}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{fak-ka-ra}, not \emph{fa-ka-ra}. You met it among the ḥarakāt and on the tail of \emph{shukran}; here it is load-bearing, because that doubling is the whole difference between one verb and another.

Everyday Arabic prints no \emph{shadda}, as it prints no short vowels; the reader supplies it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{فَكَّرَ}} (\emph{fakkara}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{he thought}, he pondered.\textquotedblright{} Root \textbf{\ar{ف}-\ar{ك}-\ar{ر}}.

Doubling a root's middle consonant is no irregularity. It is a pattern with a name and a job: \textbf{\ar{فَعَّلَ}} (\emph{faʿʿala}), which grammarians number \textbf{Form II}, and it generally means doing the root \textbf{hard}, \textbf{repeatedly}, or \textbf{to something else}. \emph{Fakkara} is thinking worked at, while the bare root holds the raw material:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{فِكْر}} (\emph{fikr}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{thought},\textquotedblright{} thinking as such.
  \item \textbf{\ar{فِكْرة}} (\emph{fikra}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{an idea},\textquotedblright{} one thought, closed by the same \textbf{\ar{ة}} that made a library out of an office.
  \item \textbf{\ar{تَفْكير}} (\emph{tafkīr}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{thinking},\textquotedblright{} the activity, on Form II's own noun shape.
  \item \textbf{\ar{مُفَكِّر}} (\emph{mufakkir}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a thinker}.\textquotedblright{} Form II builds its doer with a \textbf{\ar{مُ}} (\emph{mu-}) prefix, not the long \emph{ā} of \emph{kātib}. A rebuilt verb gets a rebuilt doer.
\end{itemize}

No English cousin here, and no Hebrew twin worth the claim.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the doubling — fa-ka-ra, then fak-ka-ra, shadda on the kāf
  \item \textquotedblleft{}fakkara,\textquotedblright{} he thought — then fikr, thought; fikra, an idea
  \item plain beside rebuilt — ʾakhadha, then fakkara
  \item the two doers — kātib, a writer; mufakkir, a thinker
  \item the done-to shape holding steady — maktūb, maʾkhūdh
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the \textbf{shadda} instruct, and which letter carries it in \textbf{\ar{فَكَّرَ}}? (\textbf{Double the consonant} — it rides the \textbf{\ar{ك}}.) What is Form II, and what does it do to a root? (\textbf{\ar{فَعَّلَ}}, middle letter \textbf{doubled} — the root done hard, repeatedly, or to something else.) How does Form II build its doer, against \emph{kataba} and \emph{ʾakhadha}? (\textbf{\ar{مُفَكِّر}} with \textbf{mu-}, against \textbf{\ar{كاتِب}} and \textbf{\ar{آخِذ}} with a long \emph{ā}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sāʿada]{\ar{ساعد} (sāʿada) — \textquotedblleft{}he helped,\textquotedblright{} from a root meaning good fortune}

\label{lesson:AR-C32-saada}



\begin{quote}
The second way Arabic rebuilds a root is gentler than doubling: it stretches a vowel. What comes out is a verb pointed at somebody else.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Nothing new: \textbf{\ar{س}} (\emph{sīn}), \textbf{\ar{ا}} (\emph{alif}, here carrying long \emph{ā}), \textbf{\ar{ع}} (\emph{ʿayn}) and \textbf{\ar{د}} (\emph{dāl}).

Two things are worth noticing. \textbf{\ar{ساعد}} breaks in two — \textbf{\ar{سا}}, then \textbf{\ar{عد}} — because \emph{alif} will not join forwards, the split that broke \textbf{\ar{أخذ}} and \textbf{\ar{ذهب}} while \textbf{\ar{كتب}} ran whole. And \textbf{\ar{ع}} sits \textbf{inside} a word here, joined on both sides, where in \textbf{\ar{عرف}} it opened one: the \emph{ʿayn} changes shape by position more than almost any letter, while its throat-tightening sound never changes.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{ساعَدَ}} (\emph{sāʿada}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{he helped}.\textquotedblright{} Root \textbf{\ar{س}-\ar{ع}-\ar{د}} — which on its own does not mean helping at all. It means \textbf{good fortune}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{سَعيد}} (\emph{saʿīd}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{happy}, fortunate,\textquotedblright{} also the name \textbf{Saeed}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{سَعادة}} (\emph{saʿāda}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{happiness}.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

Stretch the vowel after the first root letter — \textbf{\ar{فاعَلَ}} (\emph{fāʿala}), \textbf{Form III} — and the verb turns outward: doing the root \textbf{with} or \textbf{toward} another person. \emph{Sāʿada} is bringing your good fortune to bear on somebody. That is Arabic's account of helping.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{مُساعَدة}} (\emph{musāʿada}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{help, assistance}.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\ar{مُساعِد}} (\emph{musāʿid}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{an assistant},\textquotedblright{} on the same \textbf{\ar{مُ}} doer prefix that gave \emph{mufakkir}.
\end{itemize}

English carries one name from this root: the ruling family \textbf{\ar{آل} \ar{سُعود}} (\emph{Āl Saʿūd}) is what is said in \textbf{Saudi} Arabia — a family name, not a borrowed verb. Hebrew's \textbf{\he{סָעַד}} (\emph{saʿad}), \textquotedblleft{}to sustain,\textquotedblright{} is the twin; a \textbf{\he{מִסְעָדָה}} (\emph{misʿada}) is a restaurant.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pieces — \ar{سا}, then \ar{عد} — \textquotedblleft{}sāʿada,\textquotedblright{} he helped
  \item which break — ʾakhadha and sāʿada in two, kataba in one
  \item the ʿayn opening ʿarafa, then joined inside sāʿada
  \item the root before the help — saʿīd, happy; saʿāda, happiness
  \item doubled against stretched — fakkara's shadda, sāʿada's long ā
  \item the two mu- doers — mufakkir, a thinker; musāʿid, an assistant
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does Form III do to a root, and to its meaning? (\textbf{Stretches the vowel after the first letter} — \textbf{\ar{فاعَلَ}} — and aims the action \textbf{at somebody else}.) What does \textbf{\ar{س}-\ar{ع}-\ar{د}} mean before it means helping? (\textbf{Good fortune} — \emph{saʿīd}, \textquotedblleft{}happy.\textquotedblright{}) Which mark makes \emph{fakkara} Form II, and does \emph{sāʿada} carry one? (\textbf{The shadda} on the \textbf{\ar{ك}} — and \textbf{no}.) Which English place-name carries this root? (\textbf{Saudi} Arabia, from \textbf{\ar{آل} \ar{سُعود}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ʾaḥabba]{\ar{أحبّ} (ʾaḥabba) — \textquotedblleft{}he loved,\textquotedblright{} and the four shapes together}

\label{lesson:AR-C32-ahabba}



\begin{quote}
The last verb of the chapter, and the last of its four shapes: plain, doubled, stretched — and now prefixed.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Three letter-shapes for four consonants. \textbf{\ar{أ}} (hamza on its \emph{alif} seat), \textbf{\ar{ح}} (\emph{ḥāʾ}, the hook family's undotted member, a hard breath from deep in the throat) and \textbf{\ar{ب}} (\emph{bāʾ}) — with the \textbf{shadda} on that final \textbf{\ar{ب}} doubling it: \textbf{\ar{أَحَبَّ}} is \emph{ʾa-ḥab-ba}.

The mark is the one that rode the \textbf{\ar{ك}} of \textbf{\ar{فَكَّرَ}}, doing a different job: there it built a new verb, here it only spells a root whose last two letters are the same.

On the page the word breaks after the \emph{alif} — \textbf{\ar{أ}}, then \textbf{\ar{حبّ}} — the two-piece split of \textbf{\ar{ساعد}} and \textbf{\ar{أخذ}} once again.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{أَحَبَّ}} (\emph{ʾaḥabba}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{he loved},\textquotedblright{} and more mildly \textquotedblleft{}he liked.\textquotedblright{} Root \textbf{\ar{ح}-\ar{ب}-\ar{ب}}.

The \textbf{\ar{أَ}} on the front is \textbf{Form IV}, \textbf{\ar{أَفْعَلَ}} (\emph{ʾafʿala}): the prefix that makes a root \textbf{bring about} its own idea. Love, on this account, is something a person causes.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{حُبّ}} (\emph{ḥubb}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{love}.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\ar{حَبيب}} (\emph{ḥabīb}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{beloved},\textquotedblright{} feminine \textbf{\ar{حَبيبة}} (\emph{ḥabība}); add the \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} ending of \textbf{\ar{اسمي}} (\emph{ismī}) and it is \textbf{\ar{حَبيبي}} (\emph{ḥabībī}), \textquotedblleft{}my beloved.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\ar{مَحْبوب}} (\emph{maḥbūb}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{beloved, well-liked},\textquotedblright{} the \textbf{done-to} shape of \emph{maktūb} and \emph{maʾkhūdh}.
\end{itemize}

Hebrew's ordinary verb for loving, \textbf{\he{אָהַב}} (\emph{ahav}), is \textbf{not} a relative. The real twin is \textbf{\he{חָבִיב}} (\emph{ḥaviv}), \textquotedblleft{}dear,\textquotedblright{} which is \emph{ḥabīb} exactly. No English word descends from \textbf{\ar{ح}-\ar{ب}-\ar{ب}}: \emph{ḥabībī} travels through music, not dictionaries.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the chapter's four — ʾakhadha, fakkara, sāʿada, ʾaḥabba
  \item the four shapes — plain, doubled, stretched, ʾa- prefix
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ʾaḥabba,\textquotedblright{} he loved — then ḥubb, love; ḥabīb, beloved
  \item the pieces — \ar{أ} alone, then \ar{حبّ}, as \ar{ساعد} split into \ar{سا} and \ar{عد}
  \item the done-to run — maktūb, maʾkhūdh, maḥbūb
  \item the ma- place shape from the first verb lesson — madhhab, maktab
  \item the rebuilt doers — mufakkir; musāʿid
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name this chapter's four verbs and the shape each wears. (\emph{\textbf{ʾAkhadha}} plain, \emph{\textbf{fakkara}} doubled, \emph{\textbf{sāʿada}} stretched, \emph{\textbf{ʾaḥabba}} prefixed — Forms I to IV.) What does Form IV's \textbf{\ar{أَ}} do? (\textbf{Makes the root bring about its own idea}.) Why does \textbf{\ar{أحبّ}} carry a shadda, and is it \emph{fakkara}'s reason? (\textbf{Because the root's last two letters are both \ar{ب}} — \textbf{not} a Form II doubling.) Which Hebrew word is \emph{ḥabīb}, and which root first showed you the \emph{ma-} shapes? (\emph{\textbf{\he{חָבִיב}}} — while \emph{ahav} is no relation — and \textbf{\ar{ذ}-\ar{ه}-\ar{ب}}, in \emph{madhhab}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
